newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - Slim majority see Fed tightening in Nov.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Slim majority see Fed tightening in Nov.

text.p: The Federal Reserve is expected to raise interest rates in November to pre-empt upward pressure on inflation, a slim majority of Wall Street pundits said in a Reuters survey.
Seventeen out of 32 economists interviewed said they see the Fed tightening credit at the next meeting of its Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on November 13.
All but one of the 17 economists called for a 25 basis-point hike in the federal funds rate. Nikko Securities analysts see the Fed raising the rate by half a percentage point.
The federal funds rate is currently targeted by the Fed at 5.25 percent. The discount rate is at 5.0 percent.
Of the remaining 15 respondents, three said there was a 50 percent chance the Fed would tighten policy and 12 said they expected the Fed to stand pat at the November meeting.

Those expecting no move in November ended up forming a diverse group, whose opinions for the next change in monetary policy ranged from a tightening in December 1996 to an easing in the first quarter of 1997 to no move until 1998.

Inflation was the biggest fear of those calling for a Fed tightening in November. "The Fed's got to tighten policy," said Charles Lieberman, managing director and director of financial markets research at Chase Securities Inc.
"They're moving slowly, so when bad news materializes they will have to move more rapidly ... (But) once the ice is broken, they will be less inhibited from moving again," Lieberman added.
Some also expressed concerns about specific strong sectors of the U.S. economy.

"With numbers that continue to be strong in some sectors of the economy, like housing, the Fed may be forced to tighten," said David Berson, chief economist, Federal National Mortgage Association (Fannie Mae).
Analysts said that if the Fed tightens monetary policy in November, the move will likely be interpreted as one of a series and not as a one-time shot.
From a money market perspective, analysts said the recent rise in yields in the short-end of the curve was already an indication the market might be expecting a Fed move.
"Basically, the short end moved up. We see the Fed tightening after the election -- two or three upward moves," said David Wyss, research director at DRI/McGraw Hill.

Wyss said, however, that bond yields could ease a bit after the economy shows further evidence of slowing down. "By the spring we'll start seeing slower growth and the bond yield will start easing a bit," he said.
